newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian economy looking rosier despite GDP queries.
newsitem.headline: Russian economy looking rosier despite GDP queries.

text.p: Financial analysts agreed with premier Viktor Chernomyrdin's upbeat assessment of the Russian economy on Wednesday, though most doubted his claim that GDP leaped in the first half and few saw the stock market jumping.
"It's a very slippery figure," said CentreInvest Securities research chief James Fenkner of the prime minister's assertion that official gross domestic product rose one percent from January to June.
"Yes, it could be done, but the market tends not to move on GDP, just because a lot of activity is not reported."

Controversy has swirled around Russia's GDP figures since the State Statistics Committee first reported 0.1 percent month on month growth in January, the first time the Russian economy showed signs of pulling out of the steep and prolonged decline begun when Soviet communism collapsed in 1991.

Independent analysts accused the statistics committee of cooking the books, increasing the weight given to the dynamic unofficial economy without adjusting comparative figures, while statisticians denied any change in methodology.

But while analysts said they doubted figures for the first half of the year, yet to be formally released, would show major GDP growth, they were bullish on Russia's economic health as President Boris Yeltsin ends the first year of his second term.
Leading Russian stocks powered to record highs on Thursday on what traders said was a wave of new money from Western investors, increasingly optimistic about Russia's future.

"Almost any engineering company, any real Russian company has been moving in share price," said Fenkner, pointing to growing investor interest in Russian companies that did not depend on exports or monopoly status to survive.
"They're being rewarded for survival," he said.

With a dynamic young team of reformers staffing his cabinet, Yeltsin is anxious to show they are hacking through the tangle of non-payments choking the economy and producing concrete results from the often painful reforms they are pushing through.

Trillions of roubles (billions of dollars) in pension arrears were paid off this week, a red-letter event made possible partly as a result of the government's drive to squeeze yet more trillions of unpaid taxes out of reluctant companies.

And Yeltsin has ordered the government to settle debts to the demoralised armed forces within two months and pay off wage arrears to long-suffering state employees, many of whom have not been paid for months, by October.
But the drive is more than just political showmanship, analysts say.
"I think a more credible thing is that they paid off pensions," said Creditanstalt Grant director of research Tom Balestrery.
"That's a more credible sign of commitment to reform than some statement about GDP growth so long as they're not heroic in claiming to accomplish what they can't."
And while analysts said paying off wage arrears and breaking the cycle of intercompany and government debt would be tougher than settling up with pensioners, it would not be impossible.
"With the help of the World Bank, a lot of it will happen," said CentreInvest's Fenkner, referring to a recent $800 million loan from the bank to fund social restructuring.

And the government's efforts to tackle the natural monopolies, like natural gas producer Gazprom and national power company UES, were also beginning to look promising, said Balestrery, although he said there was a long way to go yet.

"Employees nationwide will have wages paid when industrial companies see a lowering in energy costs and therefore will be able to pay taxes, employees and suppliers and invest in growth," he said. "I would see definite progress (on non-payments) in six to 12 months."
--Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
